# [Objective](#toc.xhtml_s192a)

After reading this chapter, the reader will be able to know the different types of partitions as well as configurations of RAIDs levels.

We know that hard disk stores data and retrieves it when needed. When you are planning to install the operating system on hardware, then it is mandatory to define the file system on the disk according to requirements. The dual boot of operating system requires the partition layout along with file system, and what should be the file system for installing Linux as well as non-Linux operating system. That’s why we need to study the partitions and file system. The purpose of describing the RAID levels is how to use fault tolerance if any of the disks failed.

# [General introduction to partition](#toc.xhtml_s193a)

There are three kinds of partitions: primary, extended, and logical. You can create a maximum of four primary partitions which are directly written to hard drive. After creating four partitions, you cannot create any extended/logical partition. You can create three primary partitions along with one extended. In extended partition you can create logical partitions, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).1](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_1)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).1.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).1:** Logical representation of partitions

You can create a partition by the following two methods:

*   **Graphical User Interface** (**GUI**)

    To access the GUI, log in to the Linux system using username and password and then in GUI, go to **`Application`** | **`Utilities`**, and click on **`Disk`**.

*   **Command Line Interface** (**CLI**)

    To access the CLI, log in to the Linux system using username and password and then right click on the blank area of the desktop. Then, go to **`Open terminal`** option. This process is applicable on CentOS7 and for CentOS8\. Click on **`Activities,`** then click on icon ![](images/Image34583.jpg) or type **`terminal`** on search box. Now, type **`fdisk`** or parted as you want.

# [Lab preparation process using Oracle Virtual Box](#toc.xhtml_s194a)

To perform the task related to partitions/LVMs, we should first know the process to adding the spare disk on virtual machine. The steps are given below.

First of all, Shutdown VM and then right click on VM. Then, go to **`Settings`** | **`Storage`** and select a controller. Click on **`Add hard-disk`** | **`Create`**, now select size of your choice (in this demo 10 GB is taken). Now, this hard disk will appear on the storage list in the settings window.

**As one main hard disk is already there, you cannot add additional 4 hard disk to an IDE controller. Hence, first you have to add a SATA controller or SCSI controller. SDA represents the main hard disk in which OS is installed. Avoid experimenting with this until you understand clearly.**

# [Step-by-step process of creating a partition](#toc.xhtml_s195a)

The following are the steps to create partition on the disk using the **`fdisk`** utility. The number of switches is available in **`fdisk`** utility. You can find more about the **`fdisk`** using the command **`man fdisk`**:

1.  First, add storage to virtualization platform (VMware/Oracle Virtual box) or leave an unallocated space during the installation. Then, add the four-disk space to oracle virtual box for learning purposes.
2.  Run the command **`fdisk –l | less or lsblk`** to verify the disk space, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).2](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_2)*. The **`lsblk`** is more user friendly:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).2.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).2:** Displaying block devices

3.  Now, create a 5 GB partition on sdb or any other disk using the command **`fdisk /dev/sdb`**., as shown in *[Figure 10(A).3](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_3)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).3.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).3:** Running partition

4.  Now, add new partition using the command **`n`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).4](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_4)*.

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).4.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).4:** Creating partition

5.  You can create a primary or extended partition using the code **`p`** or **`e`**. Now, create a primary partition using **`p`**. To accept all default values, press *Enter* key after it assigns +5 GB partition space and then press *Enter* key again, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).5](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_5)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).5.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).5:** Assigning primary partition

6.  Run the command **`w`** to accept all changes, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).6](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_6)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).6.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).6:** Applying changes

7.  Run the **`partprobe`** command. The **`partprobe`** command informs the operating system that partition table changed, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).7](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_7)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).7.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).7:** Applying changes

8.  Run the command **`lsblk`** to verify the location of partition. Now, assign the file system to a newly partition disk using the command **`mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1`** and wait for seconds, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).8](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_8)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).8.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).8:** Displaying block devices

# [Step-by-step method of assigning a file system on partition](#toc.xhtml_s196a)

You can assign the file system on partition disk using the **`mkfs`** utility. The syntax for using **`mkfs`** command is **`mkfs.<file system> <Disk path>`**. Now, using the syntax, run the command **`mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).9](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_9)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).9.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).9:** Assigning file system

Run the command **`fdisk -l /dev/sdb`** to check the Linux partition. *[Figure 10(A).10](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_10)* displays that **`Id=83`** which means it is a Linux Partition:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).10.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).10:** Displaying partitioned disk

# [Mounting the file system using /etc/fstab](#toc.xhtml_s197a)

The **`/etc/fstab`** file contains the information about all available partitions. The mounting point remains available even if the system is restarted. If mounting is done using mount command, the mounting point will be lost when the system reboots. The **`fstab`** contains six columns, each column has specific information about the partitions and file systems. Make a backup copy of **`fstab`** file before editing. The **`/etc/fstab`** information is given in the table **`/etc/fstab`** as shown below:

| **Column-1** | **Column-2** | **Column-3** | **Column-4** | **Column-5** | **Column-6** |
| Device name, that is, **`/dev/sda1`** or it can be UUIDs | Device Mount point, that is, **`/home`** or user created directory | File System type, that is, EXT2, EXT3, EXT4 or XFS, etc. | The defaults option contains **`rw`**, **`suid`**, **`dev`**, **`exec`**, **`auto`**, **`nouser`**, **`async`**, or **`_netdev`** | Backup purpose 0=no backup1= Dump back utility for partitions. Now, it is obsolete. It is used in UNIX system. | 0 means that fsck will not check the file system. Greater than 0 means check the order. The root file system will be 1 and other partitions set to 2. |

**Table 10(A).1:** /etc/fstab information

1.  Create a directory under root using the command **`mkdir /partdir`**, and mount this directory with newly partition disk UUIDs in **`/etc/fstab`**. Hence, first find the UUID of disk using the command **`blkid`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).11](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_11)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).11.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).11:** Creating directory and UUID

2.  Copy the **`/dev/sdb1 UUID`** and paste in **`/etc/fstab`**. You can mount the partition using the **`/dev/sdb1`**. In another way, to mount the partitions, use UUIDs because UUID never changed even though you change the storage slot or location. Open the file **`vi /etc/fstab`** and to save and exit, use *Esc* + **`:wq`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).12](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_12)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).12.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).12:** Mounting partition

3.  Run the following command as shown in *[Figure 10(A).13](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_13)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).13.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).13:** Mounting all partition and reloading daemon

4.  Run the command **`df –HT`** to verify if the partition is mounted or not, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).14](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_14)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).14.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).14:** Displaying partition information

5.  Now, create a file on mounted directory (**`/partdir`**) where the file will be created, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).15](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_15):*

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).15.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).15:** Creating and displaying file

# [Creating an extended partition using fdisk](#toc.xhtml_s198a)

You can divide the disk into more logical partitions using extended partition. We may create extended partition even after one primary partition. If you create a four primary partition on disk, then you cannot create more logical partition. Hence, rest of the disk space will not be available for use. Each disk has at least one primary partition. The following steps are used to create extended partition:

1.  First, run the command **`lsblk`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).16](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_16)*, to check the availability of free disk space to create partition:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).16.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).16:** Displaying Block devices

2.  To create an extended partition, select the **`disk sdb`**. Primary partition is already created on sdb and on the rest of the disk space, we will assign the extended partition. Run the command as shown in *[Figure 10(A).17](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_17)*:

    **`fdisk /dev/sdb`**

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).17.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).17:** Creating partition

3.  Run the **`w`** command and after that, run the **`partprobe`** command, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).18](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_18)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).18.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).18:** Applying changes

4.  Run the **`lsblk`** command to verify if the extended partition is created or not, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).19](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_19)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).19.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).19:** Displaying block devices

5.  Now, create a logical partition inside **`/dev/sdb2`** using the command **`fdisk /dev/sdb`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).20](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_20)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).20.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).20:** Creating partition

6.  Run the command **`partprobe`** to inform OS that the partition table has changed.
7.  Run the command **`fdisk -l /dev/sdb`** and verify whether logical partition is created or not. The code for extended partition and logical partition are **`5`** and **`83`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).21](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_21)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).21.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).21:** Displaying partitions

8.  Now, assign the file system to logical partition **`/dev/sdb5`** using **`mkfs.ext4`** command, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).22](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_22)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).22.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).22:** Assigning file system

9.  Run the command **`blkid`** to find the UUID of **`/dev/sdb5`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).23](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_23)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).23.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).23:** Displaying UUID

10.  Create a directory using the command **`mkdir /logicaldir`** to mount the logical partition.
11.  Copy the **`/dev/sdb5`** UUID and paste to **`/etc/fstab`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).24](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_24)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).24.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).24:** Mounting directory

12.  Run the **`mount –a`** command and then run the **`systemctl daemon-reload`** command.
13.  Create a file inside directory **`/logicaldir`** to verify whether it is mounted or not. If file is created, it means **`/logicaldir`** is mounted successfully with file system.

    **In MBR (Master Boot Record) maximum 4 Primary Partitions or 3 Primary and 1 extended along with 12 logical partitions are possible. The MBR contains maximum partition size 2 TB. But in GPT (GUID partition Table), there are max 128 partition with a maximum partition size of 8 ZB. The fdisk utility is used for less than 2 TB partition (often used by MBR). The GPT supports the disk size more than 2 TB. You can create 128 Primary partitions if using GPT. On GPT partition, all the partitions will be primary. The extended partition is only available for MBR. You can check the status of partition, that is primary or extended, using cfdisk tool, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).25](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_25)*.**

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).25.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).25:** Displaying partitions

# [Creating a partition size larger than 2 TB Linux version 7/8](#toc.xhtml_s199a)

The fdisk utility cannot create a partition larger than 2 TB. Hence, we will use parted utility which can create more than 2 TB partition size. It supports Extensible Firmware Interface EFI/GPT partition tables. The EFI GUID Partition supports both 32bit and 64bit platforms. The Linux kernel must include GPT support to use GPT. If you do not add GPT support in Linux kernel, then after rebooting the server, the file system will no longer be mountable, or the GPT table will get corrupted. If you want to install Linux Operating System on a GPT disk, you must enable the **Unified Extensible Firmware Interface** (**UEFI**) in the bios configuration. The GPT family tools are gdisk, cgdisk, and sgdisk. You can find more about these tools using **`man`** command, for example - **`man cgdisk`**. On many Linux distributions, parted comes pre-installed, if not, then you have to install using the command **`yum install parted`**. If your disk size is greater than 2TB, then use parted, otherwise use fdisk, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).26](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_26)*.

**`Disks Size > 2TB parted Uses GPT`**

**`Disks Size < 2TB fdisk. Uses MBR`**

**fdisk may also be used for GPT partition. Also, if size is less than 2 TB, use option** **`g`. In this way, you may create more than 4 primary partitions.**

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).26.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).26:** Displaying partition

Find the disk status using the command **`lsblk`**. This shows that we can use either sdb or sdb or sdc or sdd or sde. The disk sda is used by Linux operating system. Hence, we have selected sdc for demonstration purposes, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).27](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_27)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).27.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).27:** Displaying block device

Create a partition on HDD **`/dev/sdc`** using the command parted, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).28](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_28)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).28.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).28:** Creating partition

Now, create a GPT **`disklabel`** using the command **`mkllabel gpt`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).29](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_29)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).29.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).29:** Assigning label

Now, enter the unit, that is, MB, GB, or TB, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).30](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_30)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).30.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).30:** Assigning unit

Now, create a 2 GB partition using the command as shown in *[Figure 10(A).31](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_31)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).31.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).31:** Creating partition

Run the command print to show the present partition. To quit from parted, type **`q`** and then press *Enter* key, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).32](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_32)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).32.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).32:** Displaying partition

Now, run the command **`blkid`** to get the UUIDs of newly partitioned space on **`/dev/`** **`sdc`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).33](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_33)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).33.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).33:** Displaying UUIDs

Now, run the command **`mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdc1`** to create an **`ext4`** file system on /**`dev/sdc1`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).34](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_34)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).34.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).34:** Assigning file system

Now, create a directory **`/test`** (Under Root) to mount the partition, using the command **`mkdir /test`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).35](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_35):*

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).35.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).35:** Creating directory

Now, copy the UUID of **`/dev/sdc1`** and paste inside **`/etc/fstab`** along with mount directory and file type (to mount permanently), as shown in *[Figure 10(A).36](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_36)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).36.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).36:** Mounting directory

Now, run the command **`mount –a`** to mount all partitions mentioned in **`/etc/fstab`** and **`systemctl daemon-reload`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).37](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_37)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).37.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).37:** Mounting all partitions

To display all partitions along with mount point, use the command **`df –h`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).38](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_38)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).38.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).38:** Displaying partitions

# [Commands related to hardware](#toc.xhtml_s200a)

The following commands are used to find what types of hard drives/hardware are attached to a Linux 7/8:

*   **`lshw -class disk`**
*   **`cat /proc/partitions`**
*   **`fdisk -l | grep Disk`**
*   **`lshw -class storage`**

# [Deleting the partition](#toc.xhtml_s201a)

You can delete the partition if it is unused or causes any problems. Before deleting the partition, you must take the backup (if any). To delete the partition, the following steps are as under:

1.  You must umount it before you delete it with parted, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).39](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_39)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).39.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).39:** Releasing the partition

2.  Open the terminal and type parted. Then, press *Enter* key.
3.  Now, select the disks that you want to delete. Suppose you selected the **`/dev/sdc`**.
4.  Type the command print.
5.  Run the command **`rm`** along with partition number. The partition number you can find from step-3.
6.  Remove the entry **`/dev/sdc1`** from **`vi /etc/fstab`**.
7.  Type **`q`** and press *Enter* key.
8.  Run the command **`lsblk -f`** to verify that the partition **`/dev/sdc1 is`** removed.
9.  **Reboot, if required.**

    *[Figure 10(A).40](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_40)* shows the entire procedure for deleting the partition:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).40.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).40:** Removing partition

# [Resizing the partition](#toc.xhtml_s202a)

To resize the partition, you have to follow the followings steps:

1.  The resizepart is a program that informs the Linux kernel about new partition sizes. This command doesn’t manipulate partitions on hard drive (taken form Linux OS help file using command **`man resizepart`**). Open the terminal and type parted. Then, press *Enter* key.
2.  Now, select the drive that you want to resize using the command select **`/dev/sdb`**. Type print free, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).41](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_41)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).41.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).41:** Displaying partition

    You can also check the space using the command **`partx /dev/sdb1`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).42](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_42)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).42.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).42:** Displaying partition using partx

3.  Run the command **`resizepart`**. Partition number is to be taken from the step-2 figure. The resizepart does not change the file system, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).43](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_43)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).43.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).43:** Resizing partition

4.  Now, quit from parted console using command **`q`** and run the command **`partx /dev/sdb1`** check whether the partition is resized or not. In step-3, it was assigned 500MB space. It shows assigned space accepted, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).44](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_44)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).44.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).44:** Displaying assigned space

5.  To update the specific partition, run the command **`partx -u /dev/sdb1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).45](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_45)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).45.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).45:** Updating partition

# [Introduction to Redundant Array of Independent (RAID) disks CentOS7/8](#toc.xhtml_s203a)

It is used for data storage on server. It helps in organization for backup and recovery process. It is necessary to understand the different types of RAID levels, which is very important before setting up the server. The physical disks are connected together to make a volume group and then logical volume. It offers an excellent performance and performance depends on the RAID level according to scenario. The two types of RAIDs are hardware RAID and software RAID. You can create a software RAID using the command **`mdadm`**, if **`mdadm`** is not available in CentOS7, then you have to install using yum, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).46](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_46)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).46.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).46:** Drawing for conceptual learning of RAID

# [RAID levels](#toc.xhtml_s204a)

The following types of RAIDs levels are available:

*   RAID 0: Striping
*   RAID 1: Mirroring
*   RAID 5: Striping and Parity
*   RAID 6: Striping with Double Parity
*   RAID 10: Combining Mirroring and Striping

# [Introduction to RAID 0](#toc.xhtml_s205a)

In RAID 0, data is split up into blocks and then written across all the drive in the array. RAID 0 consists of striping, without mirroring or parity (Means no backup), as shown in *[Figure 10(A).47](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_47)*:

**`Disk requires to configure RAID 0 = Minimum Two disks`**

**`RAID 0 Volume = Capacities of Disk1 + Disk2 + Disk3.....and so on.`**

**`Fault tolerance = No`**

**`Speed = Fastest`**

**`Usages = Mostly in video editing where speed is major concern.`**

**`Storage Space = RAID 0 utilizes full space.`**

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).47.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).47:** RAID 0

In all RAIDS, while reading/writing data, both the head of physical hard drive move at the same time. If you purchase a hard disk having rpm 7200 and your old hard disk in RAID array has rpm 5400, then the resultant speed in terms of rpm will be 5400\. Hence, no need to purchase higher rpm hard drive if array has lesser rpm.

# [RAID 0 configurations](#toc.xhtml_s206a)

The following steps are required to configure RAID 0:

1.  To configure any RAID, first install the **`mdadm`** package using **`yum`** command, as shown below:

    **`# yum –y install mdadm.`**

2.  Now, check the device availability for RAID 0, whether it is configured or not using the command **`lsblk`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).48](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_48)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).48.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).48:** Displaying block devices

3.  Select the two devices, that is, **`/dev/sdc`** and **`/dev/sdd`**. Now, create partitions on these two disks using **`fdisk`** command and change the type to raid during partition creation. Follow the instructions of **`fdisk`** command or use help (**`m`**):

    1.  Press **`n`** for creating a new partition.
    2.  Now, choose **`P`** for Primary partition.
    3.  Next, select the partition number as 1.
    4.  Give the default full size by just pressing the *Enter* key two times.
    5.  Type **`t`** to choose the partitions.
    6.  Choose **`fd`** for Linux raid auto and press *Enter* to apply.
    7.  Then, again use **`p`** to print the changes what we have made.
    8.  Use **`wr`** to write the changes. And to quit from **`fdisk,`** run the command **`q`**.![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).49.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).49:** Displaying partition steps

4.  In *[Figure 10(A).49](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_49),* first sector and last sector just accept the default values. For this, press the enter key. Or you may define the values as it depends on you. To verify the block details, run the command **`mdadm /dev/sd[c-d]1`**. If no superblock is present, it means the disks have no previous RAID partition in the target system, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).50](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_50)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).50.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).50:** Checking block details

5.  Create md device and select the RAID Level 0 as shown in *[Figure 10(A).51](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_51)*. The md driver provides virtual devices that are created from one or more independent underlying devices. This array of devices provides redundancy. The devices are often disk drives, hence the acronym RAID, which stands for a Redundant Array of Independent Disks (about md taken from Linux **`man`** command that is **`man md`**):

    **`# mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=stripe --raid-devices=2 /dev/sd[c-d]1`**

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).51.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).51:** Creating RAID level 0

    In the above command (as shown in *[Figure 10(A).51](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_51)*), stripe is used, because RAID 0 represents stripping and **`devices=2`** represent that you have used two disks, that is, sdc and sdd for configuring RAID-0.

6.  The md device RAID level 0 is created successfully. Now, check the status of RAID-0 component using the command **`mdadm -E /dev/sd[c-d]1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).52](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_52)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).52.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).52:** Displaying RAID level 0 information

7.  You can verify the RAID status using the command **`cat /proc/mdstat`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).53](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_53)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).53.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).53:** Verifying RAID information

8.  Now, check the md device status using the command **`mdadm –detail /dev/md0`**. The detail switch is used in case of checking entire RAID array, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).54](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_54)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).54.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).54:** Checking md device status

9.  *[Figure 10(A).55](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_55)* is a part of *[Figure 10(A).54](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_54)*. The output of command **`mdadm --detail`** **`/dev/md0`** has more pages. Hence, we have split the output in two parts, that is, *[Figure 10(A).54](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_54)* and *[Figure 10(A).55](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_55)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).55.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).55:** RAID status

10.  Create files system using **`ext4`** for **`md0`** and **`mount`** under directory **`/raid0`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).56](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_56)*:

    **`# mkfs.ext4 /dev/md0`**

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).56.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).56:** Assigning file system

11.  Now, create a directory **`raid0`** under root (**`/raid0`**) and then mount with UUIDs of device **`md0`**, as shown below:

    **`#mkdir /raid0`**

12.  Run the command **`blkid`** and copy the UUID of **`md0`** device and paste in **`/etc/fstab`** along with mount point **`/raid0`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).57](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_57)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).57.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).57:** Displaying block devices

13.  Open the file **`vi /etc/fstab`** and paste UUID of **`md0`**, as shown in *Figure* 10(A).58:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).58.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).58:** Mounting directory

14.  Run the command **`mount -av`** to mount all file system mentioned in **`/etc/fstab`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).59](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_59)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).59.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).59:** Displaying RAID info

15.  You can also verify using the command **`df –H`**.
16.  Create an empty file inside directory **`/raid0`**, if created means RAID 0 is running successfully, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).60](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_60)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).60.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).60:** Displaying RAID attribute

17.  As you know, RAID 0 has no fault tolerance. So, if you delete one of the partitions, that is either **`/dev/sdd1`** or **`/dev/sdc1`**, then the file will be lost. Run the command **`lsblk`**, then you will see that both drives are mounted with **`/raid0`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).61](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_61)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).61.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).61:** Displaying Block devices

18.  Now, delete **`/dev/sdd1`** and then run the command w to save and quit from **`fdisk`**. When you are at root prompt (**`#`**), run **`partprobe`** command, which will inform the OS that the partition table is changed, if any error just reboots the system. Now, try to access the data; you will find the data is lost, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).62](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_62)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).62.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).62:** Deleting the partition

19.  In production environment, you cannot directly remove the drives. Now, the file **`raid.txt`** is lost, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).63](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_63)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).63.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).63:** Displaying raid0 content

# [Removing RAID from CentOS7/8](#toc.xhtml_s207a)

You can remove any RAID level using the following steps.

1.  First, take the backup of desired RAID level and then remove.
2.  To check list of block devices, run the command **`lsblk`**. It shows **`raid0`** configuration, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).64](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_64)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).64.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).64:** Displaying Block level device

3.  First, **`umount`** the **`/dev/md0`** using the command **`umount /dev/md0`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).65](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_65)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).65.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).65:** Releasing md0

4.  Now, verify that **`/dev/md0`** is mounted or not using the command **`df –H`**. *[Figure 10(A).66](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_66)* shows that **`/dev/md0`** is not mounted:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).66.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).66:** Displaying partitions

5.  Now, stop RAID array using the command **`mdadm --stop /dev/md0`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).67](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_67)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).67.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).67:** Stopping md0

6.  Let’s assume that one of the disks failed and needs to be removed before it fails. So, now assume that disk **`sdb1`** is not working properly and needs to be removed from an existing array. Before removing the disk**`/dev/sdb1`**, first of all, we need to mark as a failure device using the command **`madam`** **`--fail /dev/md0 /dev/sdc1`**.
7.  Now, run the command **`mdadm --remove /dev/md0 /dev/sdc1`**, to remove safely the disk from array.
8.  To check the status of RAID-0, run the command **`cat /proc/mdadm`**. If changes appear, then it’s okay otherwise reboot the system.

    **All the steps work if the** **`/dev/md0`** **is not mounted. Because in RAID-0, all the data stripe means chop up and distributed across the entire disk. If any one disk fails or is removed from RAID-0, then it will not work. As we know that RAID-0 does not support the fault tolerance, so if you are trying to add a disk after mounting, it will not accept the changes because there is no parity concept in RAID-0.**

    **Error**

    **`mdadm --fail /dev/md0 /dev/sdc1`**

    **`mdadm: set device faulty failed for /dev/sdc1: Device or resource busy`**

If the devices are removed from array, then **`mdstat`** should show no RAID disk. Use the following command:

**`#cat /proc/mdstat`**

**`Personalities : [raid0]`**

**`unused devices: <none>`**

When devices are removed from array, then you have to write zero on disk to delete the old RAID array metadata using the command:

**`#mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/sdc1 No-1`**

**`# mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/sdd1 (if you want to remove second disk) No-2`**

If these two commands No-1 & No-2 (mentioned above) do not work, use the following command to write zero.

**`#mdadm --zero-superblock --force /dev/sdc1`**

The old metadata will remain on the devices but will appear older than the new metadata and so will usually be ignored. The old metadata (or indeed the new metadata) can be removed by giving the appropriate **`--metadata= option`** to **`--zero-superblock`**. For more help, use command **`man mdadm`**. After using the command **`mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/sdc1`**, you can delete the RAID partitions. Otherwise, it will create error when you try to create a new array on the same disk.

# [Introduction to RAID 1 (mirroring)](#toc.xhtml_s208a)

RAID-1 is known as mirroring. It consists of at least two hard disks. In RAID-1, the same data is copied on both disks to achieve data redundancy. The utilization rate of hard disk capacity is the lowest, that is, only 50%, so the cost will be highest, as shown in *Figure 10.68*:

**`Disk requires to configure RAID-1 = Minimum Two disks`**

**`Fault tolerance = Yes (Exact copy of data available on other disk)`**

**`Speed = Lesser then RAID-0`**

**`Usages = Suitable for scenarios where high data security requires, such as storing database data files.`**

**`Storage Space = RAID-1 utilizes 50% space.`**

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).68.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).68:** Showing RAID-1 concept

# [Steps-by-step configuration of RAID-1](#toc.xhtml_s209a)

You can configure the RAID-1 using the following steps. The theory part we have already discussed:

1.  First, check if the **`mdadm`** package is available or not using the command **`rpm query mdadm`**. If available, then it’s okay, otherwise, use the following command to install:

    **`# yum –y install mdadm`**

2.  Now, check the device availability for the RAID-1 configuration using the command **`lsblk –f`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).69](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_69)*. The disks starting from sdb to sdg are available for RAID-1 configuration. Now, select two disks sdb and sdc:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).69.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).69:** Displaying block devices

3.  Select the two devices , that are, **`/dev/sdb`** and **`/dev/sdc`**. Now, create partitions on these two drives using **`fdisk`** command and change the type to raid during partition creation. Follow the instruction of **`fdisk`** command or use m for help. In the first sector and last sector, just accept the default values and press *Enter* key. Or you may define the values in terms of kilobytes, megabytes or gigabytes, it depends on you.

    **Make sure that partitions used for stripe or mirroring are of exactly the same size.**

    1.  Press **`n`** for creating new partition.
    2.  Now, choose **`P`** for Primary partition.
    3.  Next, select the partition number as 1.
    4.  Give the default full size by just pressing *Enter* key two times.
    5.  Type **`t`** to choose the partitions.
    6.  Choose **`fd`** for Linux raid auto and press *Enter* to apply.
    7.  Then again, use **`p`** to print the changes that we have made.
    8.  Use **`w`** to write the changes.

    Using the above step-3, we have shown all procedures from 1 to 8 at one place, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).70](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_70)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).70.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).70:** Creating partition

**Same steps you can apply on sdc disk to RAID partition.**

1.  The partitions are created successfully, now, verify the changes on both sdc & sdd drives using the command **`mdadm`** and also confirm the RAID type as shown in *[Figure 10(A).71](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_71)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).71.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).71:** Displaying changes on partition

    The alternative of the switch **`–E`**, which is mentioned in step-4, is **`--examine`** as used in command **`mdadm - -examine /dev/sd[b-c]`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).72](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_72)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).72.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).72:** Displaying changes on partition

2.  To verify the block details run the command **`mdadm -E /dev/sd[c-d]1`**. If no superblock is present, it means the disk has no previous RAID partition in the target system, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).73](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_73)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).73.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).73:** Displaying block information

3.  Create **`md`** device and select the RAID Level 1, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).74](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_74)*. The **`md`** driver provides virtual devices that are created from one or more independent underlying devices:

    **`# mdadm --create /dev/md1 --level=mirror --raid-devices=2 /dev/sd[b-c]1`**

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).74.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).74:** Creating RAID-1

4.  Now, verify the RAID status using the command **`cat /proc/mdstat`**. The RAID-1 resync process is in progress and will take some time. When you run the **`cat /proc/mdstat`** again and again, it shows the time required to finish the job, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).75](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_75)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).75.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).75:** Displaying status of RAID creation

5.  The **`md`** device RAID level 1 is created successfully. Now, check the status of RAID level using the command **`mdadm -E /dev/sd[b-c]1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).76](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_76)*.

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).76.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).76:** Displaying RAID-1

6.  To verify the status of md devices, run the command **`mdadm –detail /dev/md1`**. The command will print contents of the metadata. The difference between **`--examine`** and **`–detail`** switches are as under.

    **`--examine`** applies to devices that are components of an array, while **`--detail`** applies to an entire array that is currently active, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).77](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_77)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).77.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).77:** Displaying entire array information

    The device **`/dev/md1`** represents the entire array of RAID-1 while **`/dev/sdb1`** and **`/dev/sdc1`** represents the component of array.

7.  Create files system using **`ext4`** for **`md1`** and mount under directory **`/test`** (make a directory under **`/`** using command **`mkdir /test`** shown below:

    **`# mkfs.ext4 /dev/md1`**

8.  Now, mount the md1 under the **`/test`** directory using the command **`mount /dev/md1 /test`** or run **`mount –av`**. To mount permanently, use **`/etc/fstab`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).78](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_78)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).78.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).78:** Mounting directory

    To mount all file system present inside **`/etc/fstab`**, use the command **`mount –av`** (switch **`-a`** for all file system and **`v`** for verbose mode. The verbose mode displays the details about the process of mount utility, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).79](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_79):*

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).79.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).79:** Displaying mounting information

9.  Now, the RAID-1 is mounted successfully you can check the status using command **`lsblk`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).80](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_80)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).80.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).80:** Displaying block devices

10.  Now, check if space is available in RAID-1 array using the command **`df –H /dev/md1`**. It shows only 50% of the disk available of the total array (2+2) GB. This is because the same data is available on the second disk, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).81](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_81)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).81.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).81:** Displaying RAID-1 available size

11.  Now, create an empty file under the mounted folder (**`/test`**) using touch command and run the command **`ll /test`** that will display the file, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).82](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_82)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).82.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).82:** Creating empty file

12.  To verify that RAID-1 is working or not, set one disk faulty and remove from array. If you will be able to access the data, it means RAID-1 is working properly. Because in RAID-1 data is mirrored, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).83](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_83)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).83.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).83:** Assigning faulty disk

13.  Now, remove the faulty disk using the command **`mdadm /dev/md1 –remove /dev/sdb1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).84](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_84)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).84.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).84:** Removing faulty disk

14.  Now, try to access the file **`vishal.txt`** using the command **`cat vishal.txt`** which is an empty file, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).85](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_85)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).85.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).85:** Displaying files contents

15.  Now, check the status of RAID-1 using the command **`cat /proc/mdstat`**. The RAID-1 is active under single device that is **`sdc1`**. If it shows **`_U`**,**`it`**, means device is down/ missing. if it shows **`U`**, it means the device is UP not missing/down. This proves that data is available due to mirroring. The 2/1 shows that 2 drives are in the array, but only 1 is up, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).86](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_86)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).86.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).86:** Displaying RAID status

16.  We have already removed (in step-16) sdb from RAID-1 array and added the new disk sde for showing how RAID-1 works after removal/addition of the disk. Now, add the device sde using the command **`mdadm /dev/md1 –add /dev/sde`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).87](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_87)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).87.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).87:** Adding disk in RAID array

17.  Now, find the present array size using the command **`mdadm --detail /dev/md1`**. The total number of devices available in the array are two (because we added one spare), as shown in *[Figure 10(A).88](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_88)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).88.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).88:** Displaying RAID information

18.  Now, grow (or shrink) an array, or otherwise reshape using the command **`mdadm --grow --raid-devices=2 /dev/md1`**. But when you run this command, it will show that **`mdadm: /dev/md1: no change requested`** (because one spare disk sde is already added to the array). When you run the command **`mdadm --grow --raid-devices=4 /dev/md1 --add /dev/sdf /dev/sdg`**, the sdf device is added with a grow parameter. To check the status of RAID-1 array, run the command cat **`/proc/mdstat`**. It will show the message: recovery in progress. In due course of time, it will be finished, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).89](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_89)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).89.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).89:** Displaying status of RAID

    You can verify the status of RAID device using the command as shown in *[Figure 10(A).90](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_90)*. It shows that recovery is finished:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).90.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).90:** Verifying RAID status

19.  To verify the status of entire RAID-1 array, run the command **`mdadm –-detail /dev/md1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).91](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_91)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).91.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).91:** Displaying entire RAID status

***[Figure 10(A).91](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_91)*** tells that the total number of available disks = 4 disks for RAID level=1 Storage Disks =2 Disks Redundant Disks =2 Disks.

# [Deleting the RAID-1 array](#toc.xhtml_s210a)

First, take the backup of desired RAID and then delete. The deletion steps of RAID-1 array are as under:

1.  First of all, umount the RAID-1 array device using the command **`umount /dev/md1`**.
2.  Now, stop the RAID-1 array device using the command **`mdadm --stop /dev/md1`**.
3.  Remove the RAID-1 device using the command **`mdadm –remove /dev/md1`**. If it displays the error which is given below, then go to step-4, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).92](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_92)*:

    **`mdadm: error opening md1: No such file or directory`**

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).92.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).92:** Removing RAID-1 device

4.  Write the zero superblocks (remove RAID metadata or its signature) on respective disks/partitions (if any) using the command **`mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/sdx,`** where **`x`** is a variable and it could be 1, 2 or 3, etc., as shown in *[Figure 10(A).93](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_93)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).93.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).93:** Releasing md1

5.  Now, verify whether the RAID device is removed or not. Using the command **`cat /proc/mdadm`**. *[Figure 10(A).94](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_94)* informs no raid-1 device appears, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).94](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_94)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).94.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).94:** Displaying RAID status

6.  Finally, remove the **`/dev/md1`** mounting point from **`/etc/fstab`**, otherwise system will go into maintenance mode when you reboot the system.

# [Introduction to RAID10 (mirroring + striping)](#toc.xhtml_s211a)

RAID-10 consists of mirroring plus striping with at least four hard disks (because RAID-1 requires minimum 2 disks and RAID-0 minimum 2 Disk total 4 disks requires). The data is written in stripe across primary disks that have been mirrored to secondary disks. The utilization rate of hard disk capacity is the lowest, that is, 50% only, so the cost is the highest as shown in *[Figure 10(A).95](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_95)*:

**`Disk requires to configure RAID-10 = Minimum Four disks`**

**`Fault tolerance = Yes Up to one disk failure in each sub-array`**

**`Usages = Fast databases, file servers, application servers`**

**`Storage Space = RAID-10 utilizes 50% space`**

**`Read performance = High`**

**`Write performance = Medium`**

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).95.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).95:** RAID-10

*   **Case-1**: If disks B and D fail, you cannot recover the data.
*   **Case-2:** If disks A and C fail, you cannot recover data.
*   **Case-3**: If disks B and C fail, then data will be available for use.

# [RAID-10 configuration](#toc.xhtml_s212a)

For RAID-10, minimum four disks are required. Select any of four disks that are not in use and to configure RAID-10, follow the steps as given below:

1.  Select the four disks for RAID-10 configuration and then repeat the steps of RAID-1 from 2 to 5 for the configuration of RAID-10.
2.  Run the command **`mdadm –create /dev/md10 –level=10 --raid-devices=4 /dev/sd[b-e]1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).96](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_96)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).96.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).96:** Creating RAID-10

3.  Now, check the status of RAID-10 using the command **`cat /proc/mdstat`**. *[Figure 10(A).97](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_97)* shows that RAID-10 disks synchronization is in process. Run the same command after a few seconds/minute (as shown in synchronization time). It displays the message sync process is finished:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).97.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).97:** Displaying RAID-10 disk synchronization

    *[Figure 10(A).98](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_98)* shows that RAID-10 disks creation process is completed:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).98.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).98:** Displaying disk status

4.  Create files system using **`ext4`** for **`md10`** by using the command **`mkfs.ext4 /dev/md10`**.
5.  Mount under directory **`/testing`** (make a directory under **`/`** using command **`mkdir /testing`**). And add the entry in **`/etc/fstab`** using command **`vi /etc/fstab`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).99](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_99)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).99.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).99:** Mounting directory

6.  To mount all file systems that are available in **`/etc/fstab`** file. Run the command **`mount -av`**. *[Figure 10(A).100](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_100)* shows directory (**`/testing`**) mounted successfully:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).100.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).100:** Displaying mounting status

7.  To check if RAID device **`md10`** is mounted or not, use the command **`df -H`**. *[Figure 10(A).101](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_101)* shows it is mounted, along with directory **`/testing`**:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).101.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).101:** Displaying partitions

8.  You can calculate the disk utilization by adding all the available disks in RAID-10 array. Hence, total **`disks size = (sdb1+sdc1+sdd1+sde1) =8 GB`**. As we know that RAID-10 utilizes 50% of total array, this means you can use only 50% of space for data storage and the rest of the space is used for backup.

# [Deleting the RAID-10 array](#toc.xhtml_s213a)

You can delete RAID-10 using the following steps. Before deleting RAID-10, you must take the backup of the data:

1.  To umount the RAID-10 device, run the command **`umount /dev/md10`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).102](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_102)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).102.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).102:** Releasing md10

2.  Stop the RAID-10 device using the command **`mdadm --stop /dev/md10`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).103](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_103)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).103.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).103:** Stopping md10

3.  Remove the RAID-10 device (**`md10`**), if any error occurs ignore it, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).104](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_104)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).104.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).104:** Removing md10

4.  Now, remove the RAID-10 signature or meta data from disks/partitions using the command **`mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/sb1`** and run the same command for other disks/partitions., as shown in *[Figure 10(A).105](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_105)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).105.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).105:** Removing metadata

5.  Delete the partitions using command **`fdisk /dev/sdb`** and the same command will be used for other disks. If you have not created a partition on disks, you can directly use the disks for RAID configuration.
6.  Now, check the status of RAID-10 using command **`cat /proc/mdstat`**. It will display no RAID disks are available for use, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).106](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_106)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).106.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).106:** Displaying RAID-10 stat

7.  Remove the entry for RAID-10 device, that is, **`/dev/md10`** from **`/etc/fstab`**, using the command vi **`/etc/fstab`**. This will open the file in vi editor. Then, remove the mount point, that is, **`/dev/md10`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).107](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_107)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).107.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).107:** Opening file

8.  If you have not removed the entry, that is, mount point from **`/etc/fstab`**, then the system will go into maintenance mode when you reboot the system.
9.  Now, verify whether mount point is available or not for the **`/dev/md10`** using command **`lsblk -f`**. If it shows mount point available, just reboot the system to apply the changes, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).108](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_108)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).108.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).108:** Displaying block devices

**Before deleting the RAID, array must take a data backup. You can find the manual pages of mdadm using the command** **`man mdadm`. This will open the manual page of mdadm which contains all information of RAID switches with example.**

# [Adding spare disk to RAID-10](#toc.xhtml_s214a)

We will demonstrate how to grow or extend an existing RAID array. For example, suppose if you are using 4 disks in an array to form a **`raid10`** set, and due to some condition if you need more space in RAID10 group, we can extend the size of an array by adding one of the disks to the existing array. After growing or adding disk to an existing array, we will remove one of the failed disks from array. You can grow the RAID without any downtime. Please keep in mind that we have already configured the RAID-10\. The following steps shows how to add spare disks in existing RAID-10 which are given as under:

1.  Now add the new disks to the RAID array using the command **`mdadm /dev/md10 --add /dev/sdf`** (This is spare disk),as shown in *[Figure 10(A).109](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_109)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).109.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).109:** Adding spare disk

2.  Now, verify that disks/partition are added or not in RAID array using the command **`mdadm --detail /dev/md10`**. *[Figure 10(A).110](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_110)* shows that disk is added:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).110.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).110:** Displaying added spare disk

3.  To remove faulty disk, first assign the disk that the is faulty using the command **`mdadm /dev/md10 --fail /dev/sdb1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).111](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_111)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).111.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).111:** Removing faulty disk

    To display the status of RAID-10, run the command **`cat /proc/mdstat`**. This will display if the failed disk is removed or not. *[Figure 10(A).112](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_112)* says disk is faulty:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).112.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).112:** Displaying disk status

4.  After adding the disk, it will sync the data from other disks. Check using the command **`cat /proc/mdstat`**. For larger disks it takes time in minute/hour. That’s why we have taken a smaller disk size, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).113](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_113)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).113.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).113:** Displaying disk information after removing faulty disk

5.  Now, verify the assigned disk as faulty or not using the command **`mdadm --detail /dev/md10`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).114](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_114)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).114.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).114:** Displaying disk status

6.  Now, remove the faulty disk from the RAID array and grow the array with 4 devices **`mdadm --remove /dev/md0 /dev/sdb1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).115](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_115)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).115.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).115:** Removing faulty disk

7.  Now, checks the status of RAID device using command **`mdadm --detail /dev/md10`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).116](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_116)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).116.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).116:** Displaying RAID devices

8.  If you want to grow the array again, all the steps will be the same as described above. We only need to mark the additional disk as spare disk in the existing array. So that if the disk fails, it will automatically be active and rebuild.

**In the above steps, we have added the disk (`sdf1`) first, then set one of the disks as faulty. Hence, the disk automatically syncs to RAID-10 group. So, no need to run grow switch using** **`mdadm`. Be careful to add disk partitions of exactly the same size and partition type** **`fd`** **as discussed earlier during configuration of RAID1.**

# [Introduction to RAID-5](#toc.xhtml_s215a)

The RAID-5 is block level striping across multiple disks with distributed parity along with data. The striping with distributed parity means it will split the parity and stripe data over the multiple disks. The array is not destroyed by single failure of HDD, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).117](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_117)*:

**`One HDD for parity`**

**`Performance = Slower due to parity overhead.`**

**`Usages = Large scale production environment where it`**’**`s cost effective and provide performance as well as redundancy.`**

**`HDD for RAID-5 = Min 3`**

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).117.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).117:** RAID-5

# [Configuration of RAID-5](#toc.xhtml_s216a)

You can configure RAID-5 using the following steps:

1.  Select the disks (min 3) as per need. For this, check the availability of disks using the command **`lsblk –f`**. In our case, we have selected the disks sdb, sdc and sdd, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).118](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_118)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).118.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).118:** Displaying block devices

2.  Now, create a partition on selected disks, then assign RAID code (**`fd`**) using **`fdisk`** command, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).119](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_119)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).119.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).119:** Displaying partition creation

3.  Now, type **`t`**, then press *Enter* key. Assign the RAID disk code **`fd,`** then press *Enter* key. Finally, type **`wq`** or **`wr`** to save and quit, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).120](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_120)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).120.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).120:** Assigning partition type

    **Perform the same steps as mentioned in above figures for other selected disks using the command** **`fdisk`.**

4.  Now, partition is created on selected disks. Run the command **`lsblk –f`** to verify it, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).121](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_121)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).121.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).121:** Displaying block devices

5.  Now, check whether the RAID partition is created or not using the command **`mdadm --examine /dev/sdb /dev/sdc /dev/sdd. fd`** is code for RAID disks, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).122](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_122)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).122.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).122:** Verifying RAID partition

6.  Check if the old RAID metadata (no superblock) is available or not using the command **`mdadm --examine /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 /dev/sdd1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).123](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_123)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).123.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).123:** Checking metadata

7.  Now, create a RAID **`md`** device using the command **`mdadm --create /dev/md5 --level=5 --raid-devices=3 /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 /dev/sdd1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).124](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_124)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).124.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).124:** Creating RAID-5

8.  Check if the RAID device is created or not using command **`cat /proc/mdadm`**. *[Figure 10(A).125](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_125)* shows that it will take some time. After a few seconds/minutes, run the same command again to check if the RAID device job creation task is finished or not. It shows that it will take 12 minutes:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).125.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).125:** Displaying RAID creation status

    After 12 minutes, run the command **`cat /poc/mdstat.`** It will display the status of RAID-5, that is, RAID-5 device created, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).126](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_126)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).126.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).126:** RAID-5 created

9.  Now, verify if RAID5 is present or not using the command **`mdadm –E /dev/md5 /dev/sd[b-c]1`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).127](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_127)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).127.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).127:** Displaying RAID-5 status

10.  Now, assign the file system on **`md5`** device using command **`mkfs.ext4 /dev/md5`**.
11.  Now, create a directory using the command **`mkdir /raid5dir`**. To add permanently, mount using the file **`/etc/fstab`** using vi editor. To save and quit from vi editor use *Esc* + **`:wq`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).128](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_128)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).128.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).128:** Mounting directory

12.  Now, mount all the file systems available in **`/etc/fstab`** using the command **`mount –av`**.
13.  To check if **`/raid5dir`** is mounted or not, use the command **`df –H /dev/md5`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).129](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_129)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).129.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).129:** Displaying partition

    You can also verify if the disk is mounted or not using the command **`lsblk`**. *[Figure 10(A).130](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_130)* shows it’s mounted:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).130.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).130:** Displaying block devices

14.  As we know that RAID doesn’t have its own config file, we have to save it manually. The configuration will be loaded to the kernel during the system reboot and then RAID will be loaded, using the command **`mdadm --detail --scan --verbose > /etc/mdadm.conf`** . If the file **`mdadm.conf`** is not present, then it will be created automatically. The cat command used to display the content inside is **`/etc/mdadm.conf`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).131](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_131)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).131.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).131:** Displaying mdadm

15.  Now, check the total space available for RAID5 using the command **`df –H /dev/md5`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).132](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_132)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).132.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).132:** Displaying partition

We have total 3 disks with space of 2 GB each. Hence, total storage will be 6 GB, but one disk is used for fault tolerance. Therefore, total available space is 6 GB-2 GB=4 GB (approx).

**Note:**

You can add the spare disk using the command **`mdadm /dev/md5 --add /dev/sdx`** where **`x`** is a variable. For example, if you want to add sde disk, then **`x=e`**. So, the command looks like **`mdadm /dev/md5 --add /dev/sde`**. You can add the RAID partition disk or directly add the blank disk to RAID array. The additional disk works as a spare disk. W hen any of the disks fail, then spare disks are automatically added to RAID5 array. The removal process is the same as other RAIDs. We have built the RAID-5 array using the three disks and one additional disk is added as a spare disk. If the total number of working RAID-5 disks is 3, then you can add the spare disk manually using **`mdadm`** command along with grow switch. First, run the command **`mdadm /dev/md5 /dev/sde`**. Then, check the status of RAID-5 array using command **`mdadm --detail /dev/md5`**. After that, run the command **`mdadm --grow --raid-devices=4 /dev/md5.`**

You can add the disk to RAID array using the command as shown in *[Figure 10(A).133](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_133)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).133.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).133:** Displaying added device

To find the status of added disk, run the command as shown in *[Figure 10(A).134](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_134)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).134.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).134:** Displaying details of RAID-5

Now, grow the RAID array using the added disk by the command **`mdadm –grow –raid-devices=4 /dev/md5`** as shown in *[Figure 10(A).135](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_135)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).135.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).135:** Displaying progress of growing RAID

To find the disk space and mounting point, use the command as shown in *[Figure 10(A).136](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_136)*:

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).136.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).136:** Displaying partition

# [Assigning faulty disk and removal in RAID-5](#toc.xhtml_s217a)

The direct removal of disk may create problems on array. Hence, first mark that the disk is faulty and remove from the array by assigning zero on super block. In other words, remove the metadata from the faulty RAID disk. The following steps tell us how to remove the faulty disk from array.

1.  First assign the disk as faulty using the command **`mdadm /dev/md5 -f /dev/sdx`**, where **`x`** is a variable, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).137](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_137)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).137.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).137:** Assigning faulty disk

2.  Now, check the status of the disk that has been assigned as faulty or not, using the command **`mdadm --detail /dev/md5`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).138](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_138)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).138.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).138:** Displaying details of RAID-5

3.  Now, remove the disk using the command **`mdadm /dev/md5 --remove /dev/sdb1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).139](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_139)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).139.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).139:** Removing faulty disk

4.  Now, check the status of the disk, whether it is removed or not using the command **`mdadm --detail /dev/md5`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).140](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_140)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).140.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).140:** Displaying sync status

5.  Now, check from the mounting point’s side, whether the **`sdb1`** disk is available in RAID array or not using the command **`lsblk -f`** or simply **`lsblk`**. *[Figure 10(A).141](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_141)* shows that **`sdb1`** is not mounted to **`/test`** directory:

    ![](images/Image1954.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).141:** Displaying partitions

6.  Now, verify that data is available or not using the command **`ll /test`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).142](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_142)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).142.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).142:** Displaying directory contents

    **We know that RAID-5 requires minimum 3 disks. Out of 3 disks, one disk is removed from array. Now, we have only 2 disks. C an we run the RAID-5 in two disks? Yes, it is known as degraded raid. It means a single point of failure; if one disk fails, entire RAID will not work.**

7.  Now, remove the old RAID signature on RAID-5 using the command **`mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/sdb1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).143](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_143)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).143.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).143:** Removing old array info

8.  Now, mark the **`sdc1`** as a failed disk and then, remove from array using the command **`mdadm /dev/md5 -f /dev/sdc1`**, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).144](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_144)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).144.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).144:** Assigning faulty disk

    Now, remove the disk **`/sdc1`** using the command as shown in *[Figure 10(A).145](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_145)*:

    ![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).145.jpg)

    **Figure 10(A).145:** Removing faulty disk

9.  Remove the /**`dev/md5`** entry from **`/etc/fstab`**. Otherwise, system will go to maintenance mode.

# [Introduction to RAID level 6–striping with double parity](#toc.xhtml_s218a)

The RAID-6 is known as block level striping with double parity. The two disks are used for parity. RAID-6 requires a minimum of 4 disks, if two disks fail at the same time, the RAID-6 will survive. This is due to double parity, as shown in *[Figure 10(A).146](#c10A.xhtml_fig10A_146)*:

**`Two HDD for parity`**

**`Performance = Slower due to parity overhead.`**

**`Fault Tolerance = UP to two HDD`**

**`Usages = High fault tolerance environment where high availability of web servers and database servers are running.`**

**`HDD for RAID-6 = Min 4 disks.`**

![](images/Figure-10(A)(A).146.jpg)

**Figure 10(A).146:** Showing RAID-6 concept

# [Configuration of RAID-6](#toc.xhtml_s219a)

The following steps show how to configure the RAID-6\. In theory, we have already discussed about the RAID-6:

1.  Select the disks (min 4) as per need. For this, check the availability of disks using the command **`lsblk –f.`** In our case, we have selected the disks sdb, sdc, sdd and sde.
2.  Now, create a partition on selected disks and assigned RAID code (**`fd`**) using **`fdisk`** command. It is the same process mentioned as RAID-5.
3.  Now, run the command **`lsblk –f`** to verify the partition created on selected disks.
4.  Now, check whether the RAID partition is created or not using the command **`mdadm --examine /dev/sdb /dev/sdc /dev/sdd /dev/sde. fd`** is code for RAID disks.
5.  Check if the old RAID metadata (no superblock) is available or not, using the command**`mdadm --examine /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 /dev/sdd1 /dev/dse1`**.
6.  Now, create a RAID md device using the command **`mdadm --create /dev/md5 --level=6 --raid-devices=4 /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 /dev/sdd1 /dev/sde1`**.
7.  Check whether the RAID device is created or not. It takes some time. After a few second/minutes, run the same command and check if the RAID devices job creation is finished.
8.  Now, verify whether RAID 5 is present or not using the command **`mdadm -E /dev/md6 /dev/sd[b-e]1`**.
9.  Now, assign the file system on **`md6`** device using command **`mkfs.ext4 /dev/md6`**:

    mkfs.ext4 /dev/md6

10.  Now, create a directory using the command **`mkdir /raid6dir`**. You can mount permanently using the file **`/etc/fstab`**. Open the file in vi editor and define mounting point along with RAID device path. To save and quit from vi editor, use *Esc* + **`:wq`**.
11.  Now, mount all using the command **`mount –av`**.
12.  To check if /raid5dir is mounted or not, use the command **`df –HT /dev/md6`**.
13.  As we know, RAID doesn’t have its own **`config`** file. We have to save it manually. The RAID configuration will be loaded to the kernel during the system reboot, using the command **`mdadm --detail --scan --verbose > /etc/mdadm.conf`** If the file is not present, it will be created automatically. To view the file, use cat command which will display the contents inside /**`etc/mdadm.conf`**.
14.  Now, check the total space available for RAID6 using the command **`df –H /dev/md6`**. We have total 4 disks with space of 2GB each. Hence, the total storage will be 8GB, but two disks are used for fault tolerance. Therefore, the total available space is 8GB-4GB=4GB (approx).

**All the processes regarding the addition of spare disks/removal of faulty disks will be same.**

# [Conclusion](#toc.xhtml_s220a)

In this chapter, the RAIDs level is explained with the help of an example. In RAID array, user has learned to create different types of RAID level, adding spare disk in RAIDs, creating partitions and assigning the file system, etc. In the next part of this chapter, we will discuss openfiler and logical volume manager.

# [LVM and ISCSI CentOS7/8](#toc.xhtml_c10b)

# [Introduction](#toc.xhtml_s223a)

This chapter deals with the introduction to LVMs, creating logical volumes, extending logical volumes, reducing logical volumes, and backup logical volume. In this chapter, we have explained the process to create **Internet Small Computer System Interface** (**iSCSI**) server on the basis of server and client model.

# [Structure](#toc.xhtml_s224a)

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

*   Introduction to Logical Volume Manager (LVM)
*   Steps to create an LVM logical volume
*   Extending the volume group
*   Moving one physical volume to new or existing volume group
*   Resizing the LVM logical volume
